note: Bz is the leading indicator and Kp is the lagging one. A southward interplanetary field is what actually opens the door, and DSCOVR sits far enough upstream to give a quarter-hour to an hour of warning - which is the difference between a readout that says 'this quarter-day was quiet' and one that says 'go now'.
Speed and density from the same spacecraft. Bz southward with a fast wind behind it is the combination worth driving for.
The G1-G5 watches and warnings, so a storm surfaces on its own rather than waiting for somebody to open the panel and check.

What the MVUM service says it holds. The raster we draw is layers=show:1,2, but a click has to name a sublayer to identify against, and the field a road's class lives in is whatever this says it is. Printing the sublayer list and their fields is the whole of what is needed to design the panel.

Three real roads out of Shawnee National Forest with every field, so the panel is written against the attributes the service actually returns rather than the ones the MVUM legend implies. Seasonal dates and permitted vehicle classes are the two the reader wants and the two most likely to be named something unguessable.
The same question of the BLM route service. It draws four sublayers and the panel needs to know which one a given line came from before it can say anything about it.
Three real BLM routes in central Utah with every field. GTLF publishes route designations - open, limited, closed, and to which vehicle types - and this is what says under which names.

The field list for Motor Vehicle Use Map: Roads, with each field's type. This is the authoritative answer to what a road's class, its seasonal dates and its permitted vehicle types are actually called - the first pass asked for the attributes and got back only the word 'attributes', which was a bad regex rather than a quiet service.

The same for the first BLM route sublayer. GTLF names its designation in the sublayer itself - 'Roads Managed for Public Motorized Use' and seven others - so the per-feature fields may add route number, surface and season on top of that rather than repeating it.

The identify request exactly as assets/js/lib/lookup.js builds it - explicit JSON point geometry, esriGeometryPoint, f=json. The probe this replaces asked a cached tile service for a feature query using an envelope, which is not something the app has ever done, and reported a failure that was the probe's own. A health check that tests a path the product does not take is worse than no check: it produces alarms nobody can act on and confidence nobody earned.

What BLM_Natl_SMA_LimitedScale actually publishes - layer 0 may not be the one. The identify feature falls through its services in order, so a broken first entry costs a round trip on every click before the working one answers.
Vermont primitive camping.
Vermont ANR trails.
Vermont recreation sites.

The identify request as lookup.js builds it, against the layer that now ships. Layer 0 is a group called IDENTIFY and refuses everything; 2 and 3 refuse too. Only 1 answers, and it answers with the fields the panel reads.

A candidate to replace the PAD-US entry that was removed for being dead. Esri's Living Atlas federal lands layer, asked with the identify request exactly as lookup.js builds it. It ships only if it answers here first - which is the discipline that was missing when PAD-US was wired.

Maryland draws nothing on the map. Its metadata says polyline and its service is alive, so the question is whether the bbox query the app actually sends comes back with features - which no probe here has ever asked of any layer. Every check so far has asked whether a service exists and what shape it claims; none has asked whether it answers with data for a real extent.

RT_DESCR reads NADA TUNNEL RD+FORESTRY RD - a road description, not a byway name, and not something to draw along a line. The service also carries SC_ROUTE and SC_SEQ, and SC on a scenic byways layer is worth reading before assuming. This asks for those values.

Asked across the whole state this time. The first attempt used a square I picked and came back empty, and an empty answer from a bad box looks exactly like an empty layer - a distinction this file has already got wrong twice. If the state itself holds nothing, the layer goes.

The same capabilities document, asked only for layer names carrying tree, canopy or tcc. The first attempt matched every name and stopped at forty, which alphabetically got as far as ExoticAnnualGrass - so the canopy layers were never in the answer. Esri's Living Atlas copy answers 499 Token Required, which is why this matters: MRLC is the public route and its CORS header is a wildcard.

The grid's own field list. A ceiling in feet is the whole point of this layer and the column holding it has to be read rather than guessed - guessing a field name has been wrong four times in this file.

The same capabilities document, filtered to names carrying conus. The first pass returned the Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico canopy layers and one bare mrlc_NLCD_Tree_Canopy, which is not enough to pick from - the lower forty-eight need a name of their own and guessing at service vocabulary is what this file exists to stop.

The lower-forty-eight canopy layer, by its real name, drawn the way the browser will draw it. The previous attempt used mrlc_NLCD_Tree_Canopy - a name that is genuinely in the capabilities list and still answers a GetMap with a ServiceExceptionReport. Appearing in a list and drawing pixels are different questions, which is the whole reason this probe exists rather than a name lookup.

The FeatureServer's own layer list. Layer 0 advertised a CEILING column and then answered a box over Lexington with no features at all, so either the grid lives in another layer of this service or the whole thing is empty. A group layer answering nothing is exactly how the BLM lookup wasted an afternoon.

How many rows layer 0 holds with no geometry filter at all. This separates an empty layer from a box I drew in the wrong place - a distinction I have got wrong repeatedly, and one a count answers in a single request.

A tight box over Blue Grass Airport itself. The grid only exists under controlled airspace, and the previous box sat east of Lexington in open country where the correct answer really is nothing. Class C came back over that same box, so this asks the grid where the airport actually is.

The canopy ramp as JSON, to decide whether the panel can draw a key for it. A continuous 0-100 percentage may come back as a hundred entries, which is worse than no key at all - so this looks before a legend is wired rather than after.

Every distinct ceiling the grid actually publishes. The fillBy map covers 0 through 400 in fifty-foot steps on the strength of what version 5 is documented to use; this asks the service instead, because a value with no colour falls silently to the fallback and looks like a styling choice rather than a gap.
Tightened from any <title> to the word itself. A soft 404 has a title too, so the looser pattern proved only that the server returned a page - not that it returned the right one.
Same tightening. This page has to actually be about LAANC for the link to be worth putting in front of somebody about to fly.
Same tightening.

Whether the FAA publishes a UAS support contact on its own page, and what it actually says. A phone number written from memory is a phone number that sends somebody to the wrong place, so this reads it off the page instead of asserting it.

The FAA's TFR list, which answered 31kB of JSON last run behind a find pattern that could not compile. This reads the shape: what a TFR row is called and whether it carries anything a map can place. CORS is the open question - it reported none, and without it the browser cannot read this however good the data is.

Whether the FAA's own ArcGIS org publishes TFRs as a queryable layer, which would draw the way every other overlay here does. Asked as a service list because guessing the service name has been wrong repeatedly in this file.

The FAA's own ArcGIS org, filtered to names that could be a temporary restriction. The unfiltered list is alphabetical and the printer stops at forty, which got as far as ILSSystemNew - so anything under T was never in the answer. The same mistake the canopy search made an hour ago.

The airport/heliport layer's columns, to answer whether the FAA publishes a contact for a facility at all. Asked rather than assumed: the answer decides whether a contact row is possible, and if it is not, saying so is the deliverable.
tfr.faa.gov sends no CORS header, so a browser cannot read its JSON however good the data is. A link is navigated to rather than fetched, which makes it the one route to this data that works.

National security UAS flight restrictions, asked across the country rather than across Kentucky and Tennessee. The regional box came back with no features, which for a layer covering a few dozen federal sites nationally is the expected answer from the wrong window - not evidence of an empty service. If the country holds nothing, the layer goes.
Stadiums, which carry a standing restriction around game time and are the one most likely to catch a hobbyist out.
Special use airspace - restricted, prohibited, warning and alert areas. Standing rather than temporary, and the ones a drone pilot has to stay out of regardless of altitude.
National defence airspace TFR areas. Asked over a national box rather than a regional one: there may be only a handful in the country and a regional window would report an empty layer.

The special use airspace layer's own field list. Asking it for distinct LOCAL_TYPE and TYPE_CODE came back "'outFields' parameter is invalid", which means those are not its columns - they were read off a different service in the same org and assumed to be shared. The columns have to be read before anything can be filtered by them.
EDW_Wilderness_01, which the folder listing confirmed exists. Its sublayers and columns, before anything is drawn from it.

Real rows from it over the southern Appalachians, where there is certainly designated wilderness. Existing, advertising fields and returning data are three questions and only the third puts a shape on a map.

BLM's wilderness and wilderness study areas - the ones the Forest Service does not hold. Sublayers and columns first, because this service is a MapServer with several and the BLM lookup has already cost an afternoon by answering from a group layer that rejects every query.

The same wilderness query asked for GeoJSON rather than Esri JSON, which is the format the overlay actually needs. This is a MapServer rather than a hosted FeatureServer and f=geojson is not universal on those - and a layer that answers f=json beautifully and refuses f=geojson looks, from inside the app, exactly like a layer with no data in it.

BLM's wilderness areas as GeoJSON, over the Utah canyon country where there is certainly some. Layer 0 is NLCS Wilderness Area and layer 1 is the study areas, read off the service rather than guessed - the BLM lookup has already cost an afternoon by querying a group layer that rejects everything.

The Park Service's nationwide unit boundary, asked directly. NationalDatasets turned out to hold buildings, parking lots, points of interest, roads and trails - and no boundary at all - and the community org listing is alphabetical and capped, so anything named NPS_ was past the end of it. Asked over the Smokies, where a park boundary certainly exists.

Special use airspace's own columns, printed on their own so they are readable. MOAs are in this service and have to come out - they do not restrict civilian flight and sit above 1,000 AGL - and the filter needs the real column name. The last attempt guessed LOCAL_TYPE and TYPE_CODE from a sibling service and got 'outFields is invalid'.

The first 16kB of Protomaps' public build, asked as a partial request. The previous attempt omitted the Range header, which asked for the entire planet archive and timed out - reported as unreachable, which said nothing about Protomaps and everything about the request. Three things have to hold at once: a 206 comes back, CORS is sent, and the bytes begin with the PMTiles magic.

Protomaps' own style package, which is where the layer names and field names live. The port hinges on these: Byways Topo reads Mapbox Streets v8 source-layers and fields, and every one of them has to map onto something here or the cartography cannot be reproduced.

What versions of the basemap package exist, and what each one ships. Asking unpkg for 5.0.0 returned a 404 - a version I picked rather than read - so this asks the registry which versions are real before anything is fetched from one.

The published file tree of @protomaps/basemaps 5.7.2, from unpkg's ?meta listing. Three attempts have now failed on paths and versions I invented rather than read - 5.0.0 did not exist, dist/basemaps.json did not exist, and the last find pattern did not compile. This asks the registry what is actually in the package and stops guessing.

base_layers.ts is where Protomaps declares every layer it draws and the source-layer each reads from. This is the file the whole port hinges on: Byways Topo reads Mapbox Streets source-layers and fields, and each one has to map onto something here. Read from the published package rather than a wiki, and at the version that actually exists.

Every attribute the Protomaps base layers read, captured as the get expressions themselves. The previous pattern looked for `kind:` and `ref:` as though the file declared them as object keys; it found one string and told me almost nothing. Roads are the half of the port with the most work banked in it - twenty of this style's filters branch on Mapbox's class values, and the shields branch on a precomputed shield field - so what roads actually carry decides the estimate.

The values Protomaps uses for a road's kind, which is what twenty of this style's filters branch on. Mapbox says motorway, trunk, primary, secondary, tertiary, street, track, path; nothing guarantees the other vocabulary divides the world at the same points, and a filter matching a value that never occurs draws an empty road class - a missing highway rather than a visible error.

Whether Protomaps tiles carry kind_detail, holding the original OSM highway value. This is the difference between eleven road weights and five, and so between an atlas you can read at speed and one you squint at. What has been confirmed so far is only what Protomaps' own default style reads, which is not the same as what the tiles contain - the schema documentation is where that distinction is published.

Every layer and attribute the Protomaps tile schema documents, read off the heading anchors. The schema in byways-style.js names seven source-layers and marks three as absent; two of those three - the natural-feature names and the surface field - are gaps the map can feel, and this is where whether they exist is actually published rather than inferred from what the default style happens to draw.

Whether the roads layer carries a surface field. Byways Topo describes itself as 'tracks and surfaces' and the unpaved marking is dropped entirely under the Protomaps schema because nothing names one. If it is there, that layer comes back; if it is not, the gap is real and should be stated in the FAQ rather than quietly absorbed.

What Protomaps calls a national park. The Mapbox style paints landuse_overlay where class is national_park, and that layer is dropped under Protomaps because the schema has one landuse layer rather than a base and an overlay. Getting the kind value right brings the parks back, which matters on a back-roads map more than most fills.

Where the names of lakes, rivers and summits live. Mapbox puts them in natural_label; the Protomaps schema marks that null with a note saying it was not established whether they are in places or pois, which is exactly the guess this file exists to avoid making. Two label layers are dropped until this comes back.

Whether anything marks a road carrying two route numbers. Mapbox tags it in the shield value, which is what says the hyphen in '23-60' is a separator rather than part of a number; without an equivalent the split cannot run, because splitting on any hyphen would cut '21/2' and every hyphenated forest road in half. The pair of half-shields is dropped under Protomaps until this is answered.
